title: The debate over formal rulemaking
summary: Trial-type rulemaking can expose factual premises to challenge, while its costs and delays may impede or displace regulatory programs.
notes:
Formal rulemaking applies a trial-oriented process to adoption of general policy: evidence is presented and tested, and the resulting rule must rest on the hearing record. The reading locates its origins in earlier agency practice and concerns of regulated businesses, then describes the practical retreat toward § 553 procedures. Wirtz v. Baldor Electric illustrates the conflict between confidential data collection and the right to test the evidence in a formal wage proceeding. The FDA’s food-standard and nutritional-supplement histories illustrate long proceedings, cross-examination disputes, statutory intervention, and partial program abandonment.

Austern and Robinson defend opportunities to question factual assumptions, including predictive judgments that cannot simply be classified as untestable policy. Dixon argues that poor hearing management, rather than cross-examination as such, may explain some notorious delays. Hamilton’s study argues that record requirements impose costs so substantial that agencies abandon programs, find alternative legal routes, or confine themselves to uncontroversial compromises. The editors also note that increasing procedural difficulty can be an intended political means of reducing regulation. These are empirical and normative arguments whose disagreement remains part of the assigned account.
